implementation_notes: Same verdict as JavaScript, with types added. TypeScript compiles to JavaScript, so the platform surface is Atomics over SharedArrayBuffer (all sequentially consistent, no ordering parameter) and the Web Locks API. There is no memory-reclamation problem in the usual sense because the GC handles it, though ABA through a reused address remains theoretically possible for a stalled worker. The blocking constraint is unchanged and decisive: Atomics.wait throws on the main thread, so a spin-wait algorithm cannot exist for the main thread, and SharedArrayBuffer requires cross-origin isolation. Use Web Locks or a MessagePort. Writing this in TypeScript adds nothing to the algorithm; the types only document the Web API.
idiom_name: Atomics on SharedArrayBuffer; Web Locks for exclusion; never hand-rolled on the main thread
pitfalls: Atomics.wait throws on the main thread - the type signature does not prevent it, so this is a production failure not a compile error.
SharedArrayBuffer is unavailable without cross-origin isolation (COOP/COEP); the constructor throws at runtime.
No ordering parameter exists, so every Atomics operation is a full sequentially consistent fence.
Busy-waiting on the main thread freezes the tab and is a user-visible defect, not merely a slow path.
alternative: navigator.locks.request for exclusion across tabs and workers, or a MessageChannel to transfer ownership rather than share
